blocks.text: New Staff: Jason Jordan

Jason Jordan has joined Brackenridge Civil Group as a Design Technician. He takes the CAD work on the roadway and site sets, and he keeps the firm's standard details and border sheets current across the active project folders. We are glad to have him.

Jason works in the engineering group and reports to Linda George, Project Engineer. Linda assigns his sheets and sets the order of his work against the project schedule. His first stretch will be on the roadway sets, where the standard details have drifted from the notes that call them and want a careful pass. The roadway and site sheets are the busiest part of the board, and a steady hand on them frees the engineers to design. Site work here is a coordinated effort: the technician holds the set together while the engineer carries the design, and the two are expected to talk through anything that does not square between them.

The practical matters are few. His station is on the CAD network, and the standard-detail library sits under the lettered project folders where the office keeps it. He plots a check print of anything before it leaves his desk. Time is kept by project number on the weekly sheet, and Linda will show him which numbers his hours land against. One rule holds without exception: no sheet leaves this office until the set has been checked and the cover sheet sealed. Where a detail no longer matches the note that calls it, he is to flag it rather than quietly redraw it, so the engineer of record sees the change. When a set calls for it, he may go out to the site with an engineer to check the drawn conditions against the ground; the office would rather he see the site than take the plan on faith. He has already shown the eye we hire for, and a mislabeled contour does not get past him.
His first task is to sit with Linda George and walk the roadway standard set, so the library is square before the next job turns.
Mark Todd, Principal Engineer
Brackenridge Civil Group Inc

Brackenridge Civil Group Inc is a civil engineering firm working out of the county seat, and it has done the same plain work since it was founded in 1996. We design the grading, drainage, roadway, and utility improvements a site needs before it can be built. Our clients are the public bodies and private builders who put up work in this part of the county: municipal public works departments, a regional water authority, and private developers. This overview sets out what the firm does, how it does it, and shows the work through one representative project. It is written to claim only what is true and no more.
What we design

The firm's work divides into a few plain lines, though on most jobs they run together. We grade a site so that it sits and drains the way it must, and we prepare the erosion and sediment control that holds the soil while it is disturbed. We design the stormwater management for a site, the pipes and inlets and detention that carry runoff away and meet the county's drainage standards, and we prepare the drainage studies that stand behind them. We lay out roadways, whether a new street in a subdivision or the widening and resurfacing of an existing one, and we design the water, sanitary sewer, and storm utilities that run beneath them. A single subdivision may draw on all of these; a drainage complaint at one intersection may need only a study and a modest fix. We take the small job as seriously as the large one.
How a project is run

A project begins with a walk of the site and a scope set down in writing, so that the client and the firm agree on the work before it starts. The design is done at our own boards and checked before it is issued. Nothing leaves this office until the set has been reviewed and the cover sheet sealed, and that order holds on every job without exception. The construction documents we produce, the drawings and the specifications, are prepared to be built from and to carry a contractor and the county's reviewers through the work without guesswork. Where a set must go before a public body for permit or approval, we prepare it to that body's standards and see it through the review.
How the office is kept

The firm is small, and its records are kept close. The drawings are held in the firm's project folders alongside the paperwork that belongs to each job. Executed agreements come back to the office, often by fax, and Mark Barrett logs each one, scans it on the flatbed, and files it with the plans it belongs to, so that a project folder holds the whole of a job and not merely its sheets. The standard details and border sheets that every set is built from are kept current and shared, so the firm's drawings look and read the same from one project to the next.
A representative project

One recent engagement gives a fair picture of the work. For {{fact:f:E-2001-001.client}}, we carried the site grading and stormwater design from the first walk of the ground through the county's review, coordinating the set so that the grading and the drainage agreed before either was issued. We offer it as one example of how the firm works and not as an account of our full book of business. We do not, as a matter of practice, discuss one client's project with another.
If you have a project

If you have a site that needs civil design, the next step is a conversation and a look at the ground. Direct inquiries to Mark Todd, Principal Engineer, who will arrange to walk the site and set a scope in writing before any work begins.
New Employee: Jeffrey Perez

Jeffrey Perez has come on as a Design Technician in the engineering group. He will draft the utility and stormwater sheets, and he is the hand the engineers will turn to when a set has to move quickly.

Jeffrey reports to Linda George, Project Engineer, who will set his assignments and his priorities. Much of his early work will be redlines, the marked-up sets an engineer needs turned on short notice. He works steadily and does not rush a callout; he checks it against the design memorandum rather than trusting memory, which is the discipline this office wants on the utility sheets. When a set goes out under his hand, he prepares the transmittal that accompanies it and notes what was sent, so the office has a record of every issue.

The first-period matters are straightforward. His station is on the CAD network, timekeeping is by project number on the weekly sheet, and the design memoranda for the active jobs are filed with their drawings where he can pull them. Every set still crosses Mark Todd's desk for review before the cover sheet is sealed, and Jeffrey has drafted to that kind of standard before, so we expect little breaking-in. The stormwater sheets in particular carry a great many small numbers, pipe sizes, inverts, and rim elevations, and a transposed figure there is the kind that reaches the field; he is to check those against the calculations and not against the last set. When a redline is unclear, he is to ask the engineer who marked it rather than guess at the intent.

The office is quiet through the end of the year, which is a fair time to learn the firm's way before the winter design work picks up. To start, Linda George will hand him the current stormwater redlines, and he can work those while he learns the firm's sheet standards.
Staff Addition: Charles Olson

Charles Olson joins the firm this month as a Design Technician. He is an experienced hand, and he will draft across the board as the work requires, setting up new sheets to the layout each recurring client prefers.

Charles works in the engineering group and reports to Linda George, Project Engineer. Linda will fit him to the jobs where his experience counts most. He knows the older conventions of the board and keeps to the firm's established way of laying out a set, which is worth more than a shortcut when a client expects its plans to look the way they always have. Several of the firm's clients have had their plans arranged the same way for years, and they notice at once when a sheet departs from it; Charles is the kind of hand who keeps that continuity without being asked.

The practical side is short. His station is on the CAD network, the standard-detail library and the client sheet setups live under the lettered project folders, and time is kept by project number on the weekly sheet. The review order holds for every set: the drawings are checked and the cover sheet is sealed before anything is issued. Charles has worked to that discipline for years and needs no instruction in it. Where a client's preferred layout is not written down, he should note it so the next technician has it in hand. He should also look over the standard-detail library with an eye for details that have fallen out of date, and mark any he finds for an engineer to review before they are used again.
For a first assignment, Linda George will put him on one of the recurring-client sets, where his memory for how each likes its plans laid out is of immediate use.
Mark Todd, Principal Engineer
About Brackenridge Civil Group

Brackenridge Civil Group Inc is a small civil engineering practice in the county seat, and it has kept to the same steady work since it was founded in 1996. We design the grading, drainage, roadway, and utility improvements a site needs before it can be built. Our clients are the public bodies and private builders who work here: municipal public works departments, a regional water authority, and private developers. The firm has stayed deliberately small, close to its work and its records, and this overview describes what it does and shows the work through two representative engagements. It is written to claim only what is true.
The range of the work

A civil design touches the ground and everything set into it, and the firm's lines of work follow from that. We grade sites so they sit and drain as they must, and we design the erosion and sediment control that holds the soil while it is disturbed. We design stormwater management, from the drainage study that stands behind a plan through the pipes, inlets, and detention that carry runoff off a site within the county's standards. We lay out roadways, whether a new street or the widening and resurfacing of an old one, and we design the water, sanitary sewer, and storm utilities that run beneath them. On a subdivision these arrive as one coordinated set. On a public works job they may come one line at a time, as the county's program and budget allow. The small job has the same claim on our care as the large one.
How the firm works

The firm holds to a plain order of work, and it does not vary it. A job begins with a walk of the site and a scope set down in writing, so the client and the firm agree on the work before it starts. The design is done at our own boards and checked before it is issued. Nothing leaves this office until the set has been reviewed and the cover sheet sealed. The construction documents we prepare, the drawings and the specifications, are made to be built from and to carry a contractor and a reviewer through the work without guesswork. The practice is small enough that the same hand reaches every job and steady enough to keep several moving at once.
Work for public bodies

A good part of the firm's work is done for public agencies, and it is prepared to their standards and their review. We take a set through the county's drainage and roadway review, prepare the permit documents a job requires, and answer the comments that come back until the set is approved. The paperwork is kept as carefully as the drawings, so that a project folder holds the whole record of a job. Public work runs on that kind of order, and the firm is built for it.
Two representative engagements

Two projects, a few years apart, give a fair sense of the work. On the earlier of them, for {{fact:f:E-2001-001.client}}, we carried the site grading and stormwater design from the first walk of the ground through the county's review. More recently, for {{fact:f:E-2004-001.client}}, we handled the roadway and utility design and saw the set through approval. We offer these as examples of the kind of project the firm takes on, not as a list of our clients or a measure of the firm's work, and we do not, as a matter of practice, discuss one client's engagement with another.
Engaging the firm

If you have a project that needs civil design, begin with a conversation. Direct inquiries to Mark Todd, Principal Engineer, who will walk the site and set a scope in writing before any work is undertaken.
New Hire: Kimberly Branch

Kimberly Branch has joined the engineering group as a Design Technician. She will draft the grading and drainage sheets, and she will run the quantity takeoffs the engineers need when they price a proposal.

Kimberly reports to Linda George, Project Engineer, who will assign her work and set her schedule. Her takeoffs will feed the proposals directly, so accuracy on a quantity matters as much as speed. A takeoff that is off by a little can turn a fair proposal into a poor one, and the firm would rather she take the extra hour than hand up a number she is unsure of. She is methodical and labels her files plainly, which is a habit this office values; a sheet she has set aside can be found later without anyone having to ask her where it went.

The first weeks are mostly setup. Her station is on the CAD network, the standard-detail library and the takeoff sheets are under the lettered project folders, and time is kept by project number on the weekly sheet. No set leaves the office until Mark Todd has reviewed the drawings and the cover sheet is sealed, and a takeoff that supports a proposal is checked with the same care. She should set up her drawing files and takeoff sheets the firm's way from the start, since a proposal is often revisited months later when the job comes in and the numbers have to be found again. When a quantity does not tie out, she is to raise it with the engineer of record rather than round it away.
To begin, Linda George has a grading takeoff queued for a proposal in progress, and Kimberly can start there while she learns the firm's file conventions.
